'''Ronnie Walter Cunningham''' (March 16, 1932 – January 3, 2023) was an American [[astronaut]], [[fighter pilot]], [[physicist]], entrepreneur, [[venture capitalist]], and author of the 1977 book ''The All-American Boys''. NASA's third civilian astronaut (after [[Neil Armstrong]] and [[Elliot See]]), he was a [[Apollo Lunar Module|Lunar Module]] pilot on the [[Apollo 7]] mission in 1968.

== Early life, education and military career ==
Cunningham was born in [[Creston, Iowa]], on March 16, 1932.<ref name="nasabio">{{cite web|url=https://www.nasa.gov/sites/default/files/atoms/files/cunningham_walter.pdf|title=Biographical Data: Walter Cunningham NASA ASTRONAUT (FORMER)|access-date=January 16, 2021|website=NASA|date=July 2014}}</ref> According to Cunningham, he intended to serve as a lieutenant commander in the [[US Naval Air Corps|Naval Air Corps]], apparently inspired by a movie around 1940, named by Cunningham as [[Hell Divers]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Stone |first=Ron |date=24 May 1999 |title=Oral History Transcript |url=https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/cunninghamrw-5-24-99.pdf?emrc=3bdc2f |access-date=3 December 2025 |website=nasa.gov}}</ref> He graduated from [[Venice High School (Los Angeles)|Venice High School]] in [[Los Angeles, California]], in 1950. The science building is named Cunningham Hall in his honor.<ref name="nasabio" /><ref>[http://www.venicehighalumni.com/HOF_MEMBER_BIOS.htm#Walter%20Cunningham Walter Cunningham ~ 1950]</ref>

Thereafter, Cunningham continued his education at nearby [[Santa Monica College]],<ref name="famousSMCalumni">[https://cdnc.ucr.edu/?a=d&d=CRS20060222.2.7.1&e=-------en--20--1--txt-txIN--------1 Famous SMC Alumni Set Forth a Path of Excellence to Follow]</ref> intending to become an architect,<ref name=":0" /> until joining the [[U.S. Navy]] in 1951. Cunningham enlisted in the Navy to serve in the [[Korean War]] and return at an earlier time than those who were drafted. However, Cunningham had to take a two-year college equivalency test in order to qualify.<ref name=":0" /> He began [[flight training]] in 1952 and served on [[active duty]] as a [[fighter pilot]] with the [[U.S. Marine Corps]] from 1953 until 1956, flying 54 [[Aerial warfare|missions]] as a night fighter pilot in Korea. Armistice discussions were still ongoing when Cunningham initially left for Korea, and the [[Korean Armistice Agreement]] was signed just before he arrived.<ref>Interview at USC Institute for Creative Technologies, June 21, 2018</ref> From 1956 to 1975, he continued to serve in the [[United States Marine Corps Reserve]], ultimately retiring at the rank of [[Colonel (United States)|colonel]].<ref name="nasabio" />

Upon completing his service obligation, Cunningham resumed his studies at Santa Monica College before transferring to the [[University of California, Los Angeles]] (UCLA) in 1958.<ref name="famousSMCalumni" /> Cunningham received his [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree with honors in 1960, and his [[Master of Arts]] degree with distinction in 1961, both in [[physics]], from UCLA. He completed all requirements save for the dissertation for a [[Doctor of Philosophy]] degree in physics at UCLA during his time at [[RAND Corporation]], where he spent three years prior to his NASA selection.<ref name="nasabio" />

== NASA career ==
[[File:Apollo 7 Cunningham.jpg|thumb|Cunningham during the Apollo 7 mission]]

In October 1963, Cunningham was one of the [[Astronaut Group 3|third group of astronauts]] selected by [[NASA]]. On October 11, 1968, he occupied the Lunar Module Pilot seat for the eleven-day flight of [[Apollo 7]], the first launch of a crewed Apollo mission.<ref name="nasabio" /> The flight carried no [[Lunar Module]] and Cunningham was responsible for all spacecraft systems except launch and navigation. The crew kept busy with myriad system tests, including successfully completed test firing of the service module engine and measuring the accuracy of the spacecraft systems.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.nmspacemuseum.org/inductee/ronnie-w-cunningham/|title=Ronnie W. Cunningham|website=New Mexico Museum of Space History|access-date=January 10, 2023}}</ref>

Following the Apollo 7 mission, Cunningham went on to head up the [[Skylab]] branch of the [[NASA Astronaut Corps|Astronaut Office]] at [[Johnson Space Center]] from 1968 to 1971. In this role, Cunningham coordinated the operational development, system integration, and habitability of Skylab hardware.<ref name="astronautix.com">{{cite web |url=http://www.astronautix.com/flights/apollo7.htm |title=Apollo 7 |last=Wade |first=Mark |website=[[Encyclopedia Astronautica]] |access-date=December 16, 2016 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081012111046/http://www.astronautix.com/flights/apollo7.htm |archive-date=October 12, 2008 }}</ref><ref name="nasabio" /> Cunningham stated that he was informally offered the position of mission commander for [[Skylab 2]], but after the position was officially given to [[Apollo 12]] commander [[Pete Conrad]], with Cunningham offered the position of backup commander, Cunningham left NASA in 1971.{{sfn|French|Burgess|2007|pp=1079–1082}}{{sfn|Cunningham|2003|p=291}}
Cunningham accumulated more than 4,500 hours of flying time, including more than 3,400 in [[jet aircraft]] and 263 hours in [[Outer space|space]].<ref name="nasabio" />

== Later life ==
On 17 June 1971, Cunningham's resignation from NASA was announced, effective on or about August 1, to become Vice President of Operations for Century Development Corp., developers of [[Greenway Plaza]] in Houston, Texas.<ref name=aanda>{{cite book|url=https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2023/04/1971.pdf|title=Astronautics and Aeronautics, 1971|publisher=nasa|date=1972}}</ref> In 1974, Cunningham attended [[Harvard Business School]]'s six-week [[Harvard Business School#Advanced Management Program|Advanced Management Program]] and later worked as a businessman and investor in a number of private ventures.<ref name="nasabio" /> In 1977, he published ''The All-American Boys'', a reminiscence of his astronaut days.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Cunningham|first1=Walter|last2=Herskowitz|first2=Mickey|title=The All-American Boys|url=https://archive.org/details/allamericanboys00cunn_0|url-access=registration|location=New York|date=1977|publisher=Macmillan Co.|isbn=9780025292406}}</ref> He was also a major contributor to and foreword writer for the 2007 space history book ''[[In the Shadow of the Moon (book)|In the Shadow of the Moon]]''.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nebraskapress.unl.edu/product/In-the-Shadow-of-the-Moon,673185.aspx|title=In the Shadow of the Moon|access-date=December 16, 2016|publisher=University of Nebraska Press|archive-date=October 19, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161019182143/http://www.nebraskapress.unl.edu/product/In-the-Shadow-of-the-Moon,673185.aspx|url-status=dead}}</ref> In 2018, Cunningham joined the Back to Space organization as an Astronaut Consultant with the goal of inspiring the next generation to go to Mars.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://backtospace.com/the-team/#wc|title=Back To Space {{!}} The Team|date=February 5, 2018|work=Back To Space|access-date=July 24, 2018}}</ref>

In 2008, NASA awarded Cunningham the [[NASA Distinguished Service Medal]] for his Apollo 7 mission.<ref>{{cite web
| url=http://www.collectspace.com/news/news-102008a.html
| title=First Apollo flight crew last to be honored
| publisher=[[collectSPACE]]
| access-date=October 20, 2008|date=October 20, 2008}}</ref> He became a radio talk-show host and public speaker, worked as a consultant to start-up technology companies, and was chairman of the Texas Aerospace Commission.<ref name="nasabio" />

== Personal life and death ==
Cunningham married Lo Ella Irby of [[Norwalk, California]], and had two children, Brian and Kimberley. Walter and Lo Ella eventually divorced. His second wife was retired Houston businesswoman Dorothy "Dot" Cunningham.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Goldstein |first1=Richard |date=January 4, 2023 |title=Walter Cunningham, Who Helped Pave the Way to the Moon, Dies at 90 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2023/01/03/science/space/walter-cunningham-dead.html |work=The New York Times}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |date=December 23, 2011 |title=Dot Cunningham says be an Angel charity touched her heartstrings |url=https://www.chron.com/life/article/Dot-Cunningham-says-Be-An-Angel-charity-touched-2422292.php}}</ref> Cunningham died in Houston on January 3, 2023, at age 90, from complications resulting from a fall.<ref>{{cite news|url = https://www.npr.org/2023/01/03/517135016/nasa-apollo-astronaut-walt-cunningham-died|title = NASA Apollo astronaut Walt Cunningham has died at age 90|publisher = [[NPR]]|date = January 3, 2023|access-date = January 3, 2023|last = Lewis|first = Russell}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url = https://www.houstonchronicle.com/news/houston-texas/space/article/Houstonian-Walt-Cunningham-astronaut-on-first-17692624.php|title = Houstonian Walt Cunningham, astronaut on first crewed Apollo flight, dies at 90|newspaper = [[Houston Chronicle]]|last1 = Stuckey|first1 = Alex|last2 = Leinfelder|first2 = Andrea|date = January 3, 2023|access-date = January 3, 2023}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Goldstein |first=Richard |date=3 January 2023 |title=Walter Cunningham, Who Helped Pave the Way to the Moon, Dies at 90 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2023/01/03/science/space/walter-cunningham-dead.html |access-date=3 December 2025 |website=The New York Times}}</ref>

== Global warming views ==
Cunningham rejected the [[scientific consensus on climate change]]. His biography page at the [[CO2 Coalition|{{CO2}} Coalition]] said "Since 2000, he has been writing and speaking out on the hoax that humans are controlling the temperature of the earth."<ref name="CO2CoalitionBio"/>

In 2010, Cunningham published a short book titled ''Global Warming: Facts versus Faith''.<ref>{{cite book |last=Cunningham |first=Walter |date=2010 |title=Global Warming: Facts versus Faith |publisher=[[Heartland Institute]] |isbn=978-1-934791-30-1 |url=https://waltercunningham.com/factsfaith.pdf}}</ref> In an editorial published in the ''[[Houston Chronicle]]'' on August 15, 2010, Cunningham claimed that the empirical evidence did not support global warming.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.chron.com/disp/story.mpl/editorial/outlook/7153663.html|last=Cunningham|first=Walter|journal=[[Houston Chronicle]]|date=August 15, 2010|title=Climate change alarmists ignore scientific methods|access-date=April 3, 2012}}</ref> In 2012, he and other former astronauts and NASA employees sent a critical letter to the agency highlighting what they believed to be "unproven assertions that man-made carbon dioxide was a major factor in global warming."<ref>{{Cite news |last=Goldstein |first=Richard |date=January 4, 2023 |title=Walter Cunningham, Who Helped Pave the Way to the Moon, Dies at 90 |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2023/01/03/science/space/walter-cunningham-dead.html |access-date=January 4, 2023 |issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

== Organizations ==
Cunningham was an associate [[fellow]] of the [[American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics]], fellow of the [[American Astronautical Society]], and member of the [[Society of Experimental Test Pilots]], [[American Geophysical Union]], [[Explorers Club]], [[Sigma Pi Sigma]] and [[Sigma Xi]], [[Association of Space Explorers]], [[CO2 Coalition]], Houston American Revolution Bicentennial Commission, Aviation Subcommittee, Houston Chamber of Commerce, Earth Awareness Foundation, and National Association of Small Business Investment Companies.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.waltercunningham.com/introduction.htm|title=Walter Cunningham's memberships|access-date=December 14, 2016|website=Walter Cunningham}}</ref><ref name="nasabio" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Col. Walter Cunningham |url=https://co2coalition.org/teammember/col-walter-cunningham/ |access-date=2023-01-06 |website={{CO2}} Coalition |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name="CO2CoalitionBio">{{cite web |title={{CO2}} Coalition Members: Col. Walter Cunningham |url=https://co2coalition.org/teammember/col-walter-cunningham/ |website={{CO2}} Coalition |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230213090749/https://co2coalition.org/teammember/col-walter-cunningham/ |archive-date=2023-02-13}}</ref>

== Awards and honors ==
Cunningham was a recipient of numerous national and international honors, including:

* [[NASA Distinguished Service Medal]]<ref name="nasabio" />
* [[NASA Exceptional Service Medal]]<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/36334648/the_san_francisco_examiner/|title='Feisty' Schirra Apologizes|newspaper=The San Francisco Examiner|date=November 3, 1968|page=28|via=Newspapers.com}}</ref>
* [[AIAA]] Haley Astronautics Award, 1969<ref name="nasabio" />
* UCLA Professional Achievement Award, 1969<ref name="nasabio" />
* Special Trustees Award, [[National Academy of Television Arts and Sciences]] ([[Emmy Award]]), 1969<ref name="nasabio" />
* [[Medal of Valor]], [[American Legion]], 1975<ref name="nasabio" />
* Outstanding American Award, [[American Conservative Union]], 1975<ref name="nasabio" />
* Listed in ''[[Who's Who]]''<ref name="nasabio" />
* George Haddaway Award, 2000<ref name="nasabio" />
* [[Houston]] Hall of Fame<ref name="nasabio" />
* [[New Mexico Museum of Space History|International Space Hall of Fame]], inducted in 1983<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/29964158/el_paso_times/|title=Space Hall Inducts 14 Apollo Program Astronauts|last1=Sheppard|first1=David|newspaper=El Paso Times|location=El Paso, Texas|date=October 2, 1983|page=18|via=Newspapers.com}}</ref>
* [[U.S. Astronaut Hall of Fame]], inducted in 1997<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/28283877/florida_today/|title=Ceremony to Honor Astronauts|newspaper=Florida Today|location=Cocoa, Florida|page=2B|date=October 2, 1997|last1=Meyer|first1=Marilyn|via=Newspapers.com}}</ref>
* [[Iowa Aviation Museum#Iowa Aviation Hall of Fame|Iowa Aviation Hall of Fame]], inducted in 2003<ref name="nasabio" />
* International Air & Space Hall of Fame, [[San Diego Air & Space Museum]], inducted in 2011.<ref name="nasabio" />
* [[National Aviation Hall of Fame]], Inducted in 2018.<ref>{{cite web |title=Enshrinee Walter Cunningham |url=https://nationalaviation.org/enshrinee/r-walter-walt-cunningham/ |website=nationalaviation.org |publisher=National Aviation Hall of Fame |access-date=1 February 2023}}</ref>

== In popular culture ==
In the 1998 [[HBO]] miniseries ''[[From the Earth to the Moon (miniseries)|From the Earth to the Moon]]'', Cunningham is portrayed by [[Fredric Lehne]].<ref>{{Cite AV media |url=https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0120570/fullcredits/ |title=From the Earth to the Moon (TV Mini Series 1998) - Full cast & crew - IMDb |language=en-US |access-date=2025-12-03 |via=m.imdb.com}}</ref>
